questions.question: In ancient India, the 'Vajjis' had their capital at Vaishali, which was ruled by the ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lichchhavis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Vajji** (or **Vrijji**) was one of the **16 Mahajanapadas** (great kingdoms) of ancient **India** that flourished between the **6th and 4th centuries BCE**.
 
• The capital of the **Vajji** confederacy was **Vaishali**, located in the modern-day **Vaishali district** of **Bihar**.
 
• The **Vajji** territory was governed not by a single monarch but as a **Gana-Sangha** (an oligarchic republic). The **Lichchhavis** were the most powerful and prominent clan among the **eight clans** that formed the **Vajji** confederacy.
 
• The **Lichchhavis** are historically celebrated for establishing what is often considered one of the earliest examples of a **republican form of government** in the world.
 
• In this system, the territory was ruled by many **Rajas** (kings), sometimes numbering in the thousands, who met in assemblies to discuss and debate state matters.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Geographical Context of Vajjis**:

 
 
• The **Vajji** kingdom was situated to the **north of the Ganges** river. It was bordered by the **Gandak river** to the west and the **Kosi river** to the east.
 
• The region was extremely fertile, making it a prosperous agricultural and commercial center in ancient **India**.
 
 
 
• **The 16 Mahajanapadas**:
 
 
• Ancient texts like the Buddhist **Anguttara Nikaya** and the Jain **Bhagavati Sutra** list **16 Mahajanapadas** that existed during the second urbanization.
 
• These included **Magadha**, **Kosala**, **Vatsa**, and **Avanti**, which were powerful monarchies, alongside republics like **Vajji** and **Malla**.
 
 
 
• **Other Options Explained**:
 
 
• **Mallas**: This was another **Gana-Sangha** located to the north of **Vajji**. They had two main branches with capitals at **Kusinara** (where **Gautama Buddha** attained Parinirvana) and **Pava**.
 
• **Kambojas**: Situated in the **northwestern** part of the Indian subcontinent (near modern **Afghanistan** and **Pakistan**). They were renowned for their high-quality **horses** and excellent cavalry.
 
• **Kurus**: Centered around the modern-day **Delhi-Meerut** region. Their capital was **Indraprastha**, and they are prominently mentioned in the epic **Mahabharata**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Religious Significance**: **Vaishali** is the birthplace of **Lord Mahavira**, the **24th Tirthankara** of **Jainism**, who belonged to the **Jnatrika** clan (another member of the Vajji confederacy).
 
• **Buddhist Connection**: The **Second Buddhist Council** was held at **Vaishali** in **383 BCE**, approximately a century after the **Buddha's** death. The **Buddha** also visited **Vaishali** many times and delivered several important discourses there.
 
• **Conflict with Magadha**: The **Vajji** confederacy was eventually conquered by **Ajatashatru**, the ruler of **Magadha**. Historians record that the war lasted for nearly **16 years**, and **Ajatashatru** used advanced military technology like **Mahashilakantaka** (a catapult) and **Rathamusala** (a chariot with blades).
 
• **Administrative Structure**: The **Lichchhavis** had a sophisticated administration with officials such as the **Raja** (head), **Uparaja** (vice-head), **Senapati** (commander), and **Bhandagarika** (treasurer).

questions.question: A 'Cut Motion' in Indian parliament is related to ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**reducing budget demands**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Cut Motion** is a powerful parliamentary tool used by members of the **Lok Sabha** to oppose or express disapproval of the **Demands for Grants** submitted by the **Union Government** as part of the **Union Budget**.
 
• Its primary purpose is to reduce the amount requested by a ministry in its demand for grants, effectively acting as a mechanism for **parliamentary control** over the **executive's** spending. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• These motions are moved during the discussion on the **Annual Financial Statement** (Budget) under the provisions of **Article 113** of the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• If a **Cut Motion** is passed by the **Lok Sabha**, it is considered a **vote of no confidence** against the government, and the **Council of Ministers** is expected to resign as it indicates the government has lost the majority support of the House.
 
• The **Rajya Sabha** has no power to move a **Cut Motion** or vote on the **Demands for Grants**; it can only discuss the budget.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Cut Motions:**

 
 
• **Disapproval of Policy Cut Motion:** This motion states that the amount of the demand be reduced to **Re. 1**. It represents the disapproval of the policy underlying the demand. A member giving notice of such a motion must indicate in precise terms the particulars of the policy which he/she proposes to discuss.
 
• **Economy Cut Motion:** This motion aims to reduce the amount of the demand by a **specified amount**. It represents the view that the expenditure is excessive or that economy can be effected in the proposed expenditure.
 
• **Token Cut Motion:** This motion proposes that the amount of the demand be reduced by **Rs. 100**. It is used to ventilate a specific grievance that is within the sphere of the responsibility of the **Government of India**.
 
 
 
• **Unrelated Parliamentary Procedures:**
 
 
• **Removing a Judge:** The removal of a judge of the **Supreme Court** or **High Court** is done through a **Removal Motion** based on proved misbehaviour or incapacity under the **Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968**, not a Cut Motion. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Amending the Constitution:** The procedure for **amending the Constitution** is laid down in **Article 368**, which requires a specific **Constitution Amendment Bill** to be passed by both Houses. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• **Dissolving the House:** The **President of India** has the power to **dissolve the Lok Sabha** under **Article 85** on the advice of the **Prime Minister** and the **Council of Ministers**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Conditions of Admissibility:** For a **Cut Motion** to be admissible in the **Lok Sabha**, it must fulfill several criteria:

 
 
• It must relate to **only one demand** and be confined to **one specific matter**.
 
• It should not contain arguments, inferences, ironical expressions, or **defamatory statements**.
 
• It must not relate to the **expenditure charged** on the **Consolidated Fund of India**.
 
• It should not revive discussion on a matter which has been discussed in the **same session** and on which a decision has been taken.
 
• It should not make suggestions for the **amendment or repeal of existing laws**.
 
 
 
• The **Speaker** of the **Lok Sabha** decides whether a **Cut Motion** is admissible or not under the **Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business**.

questions.question: In which year (AD) did the king Harshavardhana died?

• **Harshavardhana**, the last great Hindu emperor of North India, died in the year **647 AD**.
 
• He ruled for approximately **41 years**, having ascended the throne in **606 AD** at the age of **16** after the tragic deaths of his father **Prabhakarvardhana** and elder brother **Rajyavardhana**.
 
• His death in **647 AD** resulted in the immediate disintegration of his empire as he left no direct heir to the throne.
 
• Following his demise, a minister named **Arunasva** (or Arjun) is said to have usurped the throne, leading to a brief conflict involving a **Chinese** diplomatic mission led by **Wang Xuance**.

questions.question: Which instrument is associated with U. Srinivas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mandolin**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **U. Srinivas**, also known as **Uppalapu Srinivas**, was a world-renowned **Indian classical musician** who popularized the **Mandolin** in the **Carnatic music** tradition.
 
• Born on **February 28, 1969**, in **Palakollu, Andhra Pradesh**, he was a **child prodigy** who began playing the instrument at the age of **six**.
 
• He was the first musician to adapt the **electric mandolin**, a Western instrument, to the requirements of **South Indian classical music**, effectively producing the delicate **gamakas** (oscillations) essential to the genre.
 
• His first public performance took place in **1978** at the **Gudur** music festival when he was just **nine years old**, earning him the title "**Mandolin Srinivas**."
 
• He received several prestigious honors during his career, including the **Padma Shri** in **1998**, the **Sangeet Natak Akademi Award** in **2010**, and the **Sangeetha Ratna**.
 
• He was also known for his international collaborations, notably as a member of the fusion band **Remember Shakti**, alongside **John McLaughlin**, **Zakir Hussain**, **Shankar Mahadevan**, and **V. Selvaganesh**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sitar**:

 
 
• The **Sitar** is a plucked stringed instrument used predominantly in **Hindustani Classical Music**.
 
• It gained global recognition through maestros like **Pandit Ravi Shankar**, **Vilayat Khan**, and **Nikhil Banerjee**.
 
• It features a long neck and a **gourd**-shaped resonating chamber, typically having **18, 19, or 20 strings**.
 
 
 
• **Mandolin**:
 
 
• The **Mandolin** belongs to the **lute family** and usually has four pairs of metal strings.
 
• While it originated in **Europe**, **U. Srinivas** modified it into a **five-string electric** version for Carnatic performances to sustain notes longer.
 
• In the **Western** world, it is commonly used in **bluegrass**, **folk**, and **classical music**.
 
 
 
• **Tambura (Tanpura)**:
 
 
• The **Tambura** is a long-necked plucked string instrument that provides a continuous **harmonic drone**.
 
• It does not play a melody but supports the lead singer or instrumentalist by maintaining the **Sruti** (pitch).
 
• It is an indispensable part of both **Carnatic** and **Hindustani** music performances.
 
 
 
• **Nadaswaram**:
 
 
• The **Nadaswaram** is a double-reed wind instrument, one of the most popular classical instruments in **South India**.
 
• It is often played in pairs, accompanied by a pair of drums called **Thavil**, and is considered **Mangala Vadya** (auspicious instrument) used in temples and weddings.
 
• Legendary exponents include **Sheikh Chinna Moulana** and **T.N. Rajarathnam Pillai**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Legacy**: **U. Srinivas** passed away at a young age on **September 19, 2014**, in **Chennai**. His contribution remains unique because he proved that a foreign, fretted instrument could handle the complexities of **Indian Ragas**.
 
• **Global Fusion**: He was a pioneer in **World Music**, blending Indian classical elements with **Jazz** and **Western Classical** styles, performing at major venues like the **Sydney Opera House** and **Royal Albert Hall**.

questions.question: ____ concluded that not only does the earth attract an apple and the moon, but all objects in the universe attract each other.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Isaac Newton**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Sir **Isaac Newton** formulated the **Universal Law of Gravitation** in **1687**, which he documented in his landmark publication **Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica**.
 
• Newton observed that the same force responsible for an **apple falling** to the ground also keeps the **Moon** in its nearly circular orbit around the **Earth**.
 
• He concluded that **gravitation** is a universal phenomenon; every point mass attracts every other point mass in the universe by a force pointing along the line intersecting both points.
 
• This law states that the force is proportional to the **product of their masses** (m1 × m2) and inversely proportional to the **square of the distance** (r²) between them.
 
• His work unified **terrestrial** and **celestial mechanics**, proving that the laws of physics are consistent throughout the entire universe.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Albert Einstein**:

 
 
• Introduced the **General Theory of Relativity** in **1915**, explaining gravity as the warping of **spacetime** rather than a simple pulling force.
 
• Developed the mass-energy equivalence formula **E = mc²**, which is a cornerstone of modern physics.
 
 
 
• **Galileo Galilei**:
 
 
• Often called the **Father of Modern Science**, he pioneered the use of the **telescope** for astronomical discovery.
 
• He studied the **uniform acceleration** of falling objects and challenged the Aristotelian view that heavier objects fall faster.
 
 
 
• **Thomas Edison**:
 
 
• A prolific inventor who held **1,093 US patents**, focusing on **electrical power generation**, **mass communication**, and **sound recording**.
 
• Key inventions include the **phonograph** and the first commercially practical **incandescent light bulb**.
 
 
 
• **Gravitational Constant (G)**:
 
 
• The numerical value of **G** (approximately 6.674 × 10−¹¹ Nm²/kg²) was accurately measured for the first time by **Henry Cavendish** in **1798**.

questions.question: At which place was the Prarthana Samaj established in 1867?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bombay**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Prarthana Samaj** was a prominent movement for **religious and social reform** in **Maharashtra**, formally established on **31 March 1867** in **Bombay**.
 
• It was founded by **Dr. Atmaram Pandurang** with the primary objective of promoting the **worship of one God** and reforming the social fabric of Hindu society.
 
• The society was heavily inspired by the **Brahmo Samaj** of Bengal, particularly following the visits of **Keshab Chandra Sen** to **Bombay** in **1864** and **1867**.
 
• Unlike the **Brahmo Samaj** in Bengal, the **Prarthana Samaj** members did not regard themselves as adherents of a new religion but as a reformist group within **Hinduism**, drawing inspiration from **Maharashtrian bhakti saints** like **Namdev** and **Tukaram**.
 
• The movement gained widespread intellectual and social recognition after **Mahadev Govind Ranade** joined the organization in **1870**, providing it with a systematic philosophy and a broad social agenda.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Social Reform Initiatives:
 
 
• The **Prarthana Samaj** focused on four main areas: **disapproval of the caste system**, **promotion of women education**, **widow remarriage**, and the **abolition of child marriage**.
 
• It established the **Widow Remarriage Association** in **1866** and organized **night schools** for the working class and **orphanages** for the needy.
 
• In **1906**, **V.R. Shinde**, a member of the Samaj, established the **Depressed Classes Mission** to work for the **untouchables**.
 
 
 
• Key Personalities:
 
 
• **R.G. Bhandarkar**, a famous orientalist and historian, and **N.G. Chandavarkar** were other leading figures who spearheaded the movement after **Ranade**.
 
• The organization published a weekly journal called **Subodha Patrika** to spread its message across the **Bombay Presidency**.

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi organized a Satyagraha to support the peasants of Kheda. Kheda district is located in which of the following states?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gujarat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Kheda Satyagraha** of **1918** was a significant movement in the Indian independence struggle, organized by **Mahatma Gandhi** to support the peasants of the **Kheda** district in **Gujarat**.
 
• The region was hit by a severe **famine** and a **plague epidemic** in **1917-18**, which led to a total crop failure, yet the British authorities refused to waive the **land revenue** taxes.
 
• According to the government's own **Revenue Code**, farmers were entitled to a full remission of taxes if the yield was less than **one-fourth** of the normal production.
 
• **Gandhi** launched the **Satyagraha** (non-violent resistance) and urged the farmers to refuse tax payments despite the government seizing their property, cattle, and lands.
 
• The movement was a major success as the government finally agreed to suspend the tax for the year and return the confiscated property, establishing **Gandhi** as a powerful leader for the rural masses.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel**:

 
 
• A prominent lawyer from **Gujarat**, Patel was deeply influenced by **Gandhi** during the **Kheda Satyagraha** and gave up his legal practice to join the freedom movement full-time.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Champaran (1917)**:
 
 
• While **Champaran** in **Bihar** was Gandhi's first Satyagraha involving indigo farmers, the **Kheda** movement was the first major peasant-based non-cooperation struggle in **Western India**.
 
 
 
• **Other Major Movements in Gujarat**:
 
 
• **Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918)**: Focused on industrial workers' wages and was Gandhi's first **hunger strike** in India.
 
• **Bardoli Satyagraha (1928)**: Another successful peasant movement in **Gujarat** led by **Sardar Patel** against a 30 percent tax hike.
 
 
 
• **The Philosophy of Satyagraha**:
 
 
• The term was coined by Gandhi to represent a method of non-violent resistance based on **Truth** and **Ahimsa** (non-violence), which he had previously tested in **South Africa**.

questions.question: Which of the following states has the lowest population density (Per square km) as per census 2011?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Arunachal Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Based on the **Census 2011**, **Arunachal Pradesh** recorded the lowest population density in the country, with only **17 persons per square kilometer**.
 
• The state covers a vast geographical area of **83,743 square kilometers**, but its population remains low at approximately **1.38 million** due to difficult living conditions.
 
• The primary reasons for this sparse population are the **rugged mountainous terrain** of the **Eastern Himalayas** and the fact that nearly **80%** of the land is covered by **dense forests**.
 
• Within the state, the **Dibang Valley** district has the distinction of having the lowest density in India at just **1 person per square kilometer**.
 
• This demographic data is essential for the **Government of India** to determine **resource allocation** and **administrative planning** for the **Northeast region**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Population Density Comparison**:

 
 
• **Tamil Nadu**: This industrialized southern state has a population density of **555 persons per square kilometer**.
 
• **Kerala**: Known for its high literacy and social indicators, it has a high density of **860 persons per square kilometer**.
 
• **Goa**: Despite its small landmass, **Goa** maintains a population density of **394 persons per square kilometer**, which is slightly above the national average.
 
 
 
• **National Demographic Context**:
 
 
• The **National Average** population density of **India** as per the **2011 Census** is **382 persons per square kilometer**.
 
• **Bihar** is the most densely populated state in India, with **1,106 persons per square kilometer**, followed by **West Bengal** at **1,028**.
 
• Among **Union Territories**, **Delhi** has the highest density at **11,320**, while **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** have the lowest at **46**.
 
• Population density is calculated using the formula: **Total Population** ÷ **Total Land Area**.

questions.question: The universal law of gravitation states that the gravitational force between two objects is proportional to ____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**the product of the masses**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation**, formulated by **Sir Isaac Newton** in **1687**, states that every point mass in the universe attracts every other point mass with a force directed along the line intersecting both points.
 
• The magnitude of this **gravitational force** is directly proportional to the **product of their masses** (m₁ × m₂). This means if the mass of one object doubles, the force of gravity between them also doubles.
 
• The law also specifies that the force is **inversely proportional** to the **square of the distance** (r²) between the centers of the two objects. This relationship is known as the **Inverse Square Law**.
 
• The complete mathematical formula for the law is F = G frac{m₁m₂}{r²} , where **F** represents the force, **m₁** and **m₂** are the masses, **r** is the separation distance, and **G** is the proportionality constant.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Universal Gravitational Constant (G)**:

 
 
• The value of **G** is approximately **6.674 × 10−¹¹ Nm²/kg²**.
 
• Unlike the acceleration due to gravity (g), the value of **G** remains constant throughout the **universe**.
 
• It was first accurately measured by **Henry Cavendish** in his famous **Cavendish experiment** in **1798** using a torsion balance.
 
 
 
• **Properties of Gravitational Force**:
 
 
• It is a **conservative force**, meaning the work done is independent of the path taken.
 
• It is a **central force** that acts along the line joining the centers of gravity of the two bodies.
 
• Despite being the weakest of the four fundamental forces of nature, it governs the motion of **planets**, **stars**, and **galaxies** over long distances.
 
• It is always **attractive** and does not depend on the medium present between the two objects.

questions.question: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE), highlighted during a protest in early 2025 at Mantralaya, is a rare, progressive and usually fatal disorder that affects which organ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Brain**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE)** is a chronic, progressive, and nearly always fatal inflammatory disease that targets the **Central Nervous System**, specifically the **Brain**.
 
• The condition is caused by a persistent infection with a mutant strain of the **measles virus** (morbillivirus) that remains dormant in **neural tissues** for several years.
 
• The protest at **Mantralaya** in **Mumbai** in early **2025** brought attention to the lack of specialized healthcare infrastructure and financial support for families dealing with this rare neurodegenerative condition.
 
• The pathology involves the widespread destruction of **neurons** and **glial cells**, leading to severe **cerebral atrophy** and **sclerosis** (scarring) of the brain tissue.
 
• SSPE typically manifests in children and young adults, appearing roughly **5 to 10 years** after a primary measles infection, especially if the infection occurred before the age of **2 years**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Clinical Progression and Symptoms:**

 
 
• Early stages involve subtle **behavioral changes**, irritability, and declining academic performance.
 
• Advanced stages are characterized by **myoclonic jerks** (involuntary muscle spasms), **seizures**, **blindness**, and eventually a state of **akinetic mutism**.
 
 
 
• **Diagnosis and Prevention:**
 
 
• Diagnosis is confirmed through the detection of extremely high titers of **measles antibodies** in the **Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)** and **Serum**.
 
• An **Electroencephalogram (EEG)** often shows classic **Radermecker complexes**, which are periodic high-voltage slow-wave discharges.
 
• The only effective way to prevent SSPE is through universal **measles vaccination** via the **MMR (Measles, Mumps, and Rubella)** vaccine.
 
 
 
• **Treatment Outlook:**
 
 
• Currently, there is no definitive cure for SSPE; treatment is largely **palliative** or involves antiviral drugs like **Isoprinosine** and **Interferon-alpha** to slow progression.

questions.question:
Which of the following is the objective of the India’s Industrial Policy 1991?

I. To introduce liberalisation.

II. To remove restrictions on direct foreign investment.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Industrial Policy of 1991** was announced by the Government of India on **July 24, 1991**, under the leadership of Prime Minister **P.V. Narasimha Rao** and Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh**.
 
• One of the primary objectives was to introduce **Liberalization** in the Indian economy by ending the "**License-Permit-Quota Raj**." This involved the abolition of industrial licensing for most projects, allowing the private sector more freedom to operate and expand. ***Hence, statement I is correct.***
 
• The policy aimed to remove restrictions on **Direct Foreign Investment (FDI)**. It provided automatic approval for **foreign technology agreements** and allowed **foreign equity participation** up to **51%** in high-priority industries, which was a significant shift from previous restrictive regimes. ***Hence, statement II is correct.***
 
• The policy sought to integrate the Indian economy with the global market through **Globalization**, encouraging competition and increasing the efficiency of the domestic industrial structure.
 
• It also focused on **Privatization** by reducing the number of industries reserved exclusively for the **Public Sector**, thereby inviting private participation in core areas of the economy.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Both I and II.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Background of the 1991 Reforms:**

 
 
• India faced a severe **Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis** in **1991**, where **foreign exchange reserves** dropped to a level barely sufficient to pay for two weeks of imports.
 
• This economic crisis necessitated a structural shift, leading to the adoption of the **LPG (Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization)** model.
 
 
 
• **Abolition of Industrial Licensing:**
 
 
• Under the **New Industrial Policy (NIP)**, **Industrial Licensing** was abolished for all but **18 industries** (which were later reduced further to **5**).
 
• Currently, only a few sectors like **electronic aerospace**, **gunpowder**, **industrial explosives**, **hazardous chemicals**, and **tobacco products** require a license.
 
 
 
• **Public Sector De-reservation:**
 
 
• The number of industries reserved for the public sector was reduced from **17** to **8** in **1991**.
 
• At present, only **Atomic Energy** and **Railway Operations** remain exclusively reserved for the public sector.
 
 
 
• **MRTP Act Amendment:**
 
 
• The **Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act** was amended to remove the threshold limit of assets for **MRTP companies**.
 
• This allowed large industrial houses to invest and expand without seeking prior government approval for every project, fostering a more competitive business environment.
 
 
 
• **Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB):**
 
 
• The government established the **FIPB** to negotiate with international firms and approve **Foreign Direct Investment** in sectors that did not fall under the automatic route.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Impact on Economy:** The **1991 reforms** led to a significant increase in **India's GDP growth rate**, boosted **foreign exchange reserves**, and made India one of the fastest-growing economies in the world.
 
• **Technology Upgradation:** By allowing foreign investment and technology agreements, the policy facilitated the flow of **modern technology** into Indian industries, enhancing their global competitiveness.
 
• **Sectoral Growth:** The policy paved the way for the growth of the **Services Sector**, particularly **IT and BPO**, which became major contributors to the Indian economy in the following decades.

questions.question: The "Cancel Coal" case, which was seen in news in December 2024, is associated with which of the following country?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**South Africa**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The "Cancel Coal" case is a landmark climate change lawsuit in **South Africa** that gained international attention in **December 2024** following a significant court ruling.
 
• In a historic judgment, the **High Court of South Africa (Gauteng Division, Pretoria)** ruled against the government's plans to procure **1,500 MW** of new coal-fired power capacity.
 
• The litigation was spearheaded by youth and environmental groups, including the **African Climate Alliance (ACA)**, **groundWork**, and the **Vukani Environmental Justice Alliance**, who challenged the **Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) 2019**.
 
• The court determined that the Minister of **Mineral Resources and Energy** had failed to conduct a proper **Climate Change Impact Assessment** before including new coal power in the national energy plan.
 
• The ruling is particularly significant because it explicitly recognized that the climate crisis poses a direct threat to the **constitutional rights** of **children** and future generations in **South Africa**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Energy Profile of South Africa**: **South Africa** remains one of the world's most coal-dependent nations, with the mineral accounting for nearly **80%** of its electricity generation, primarily managed by the state-owned utility **Eskom**.
 
• **Constitutional Protection**: The legal basis for the "Cancel Coal" case rests on **Section 24** of the **Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996**, which guarantees citizens the right to an environment that is not harmful to their health or well-being.
 
• **The Integrated Resource Plan (IRP)**: This is a **Cabinet-approved** roadmap for **South Africa’s** electricity generation. The **IRP 2019** version was contested because it mandated the addition of new coal power despite the availability of cleaner, cheaper renewable alternatives.
 
• **Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP)**: **South Africa** is a pioneer in the **JETP** model, an international financial framework designed to help developing economies phase out coal. The "Cancel Coal" victory aligns with the national goal of achieving **Net Zero** emissions by **2050**.
 
• **Global Precedent**: The case is viewed as a major victory for **climate litigation** globally, demonstrating how courts can hold governments accountable for the long-term environmental consequences of energy policy and their impact on **human rights**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **December 2024** ruling essentially "cancelled" the specific allocation for coal in the **IRP 2019**, forcing the government to re-evaluate its energy mix with stricter environmental oversight.
 
• Legal experts highlight that this case establishes the **"best interests of the child"** principle as a primary consideration in national administrative decisions regarding **fossil fuel** infrastructure.
 
• The **Department of Mineral Resources and Energy (DMRE)** had previously argued that new coal was necessary for **energy security**, but the court found that this did not exempt the state from its **environmental obligations**.

questions.question: The '80-pillar hall' was part of the palace of which great emperor?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ashoka**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The remains of the famous **80-pillar hall** were discovered at **Kumrahar**, located about five kilometers from **Patna** (ancient **Pataliputra**) in **Bihar**.
 
• This monumental structure is attributed to the **Mauryan Empire** and served as a grand assembly hall or part of the royal palace of **Emperor Ashoka**, who reigned from **268 BCE to 232 BCE**.
 
• Archaeological excavations at the site were conducted by **Dr. D.B. Spooner** between **1912** and **1915**, which brought to light the existence of these massive monolithic pillars.
 
• The hall was constructed using **Chunar sandstone**, and the pillars exhibited the distinct **Mauryan polish**, a technique that gave the stone a mirror-like, metallic luster.
 
• The layout consisted of **80 columns** arranged in **eight rows of ten pillars each**, reflecting the advanced engineering and architectural capabilities of the **3rd century BCE**. ***Hence, the statement regarding Ashoka is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mauryan Architecture and Pataliputra:**

 
 
• **Megasthenes**, the Greek ambassador sent by **Seleucus Nicator** to the court of **Chandragupta Maurya**, provided a detailed account of the city and the palace in his book **Indica**.
 
• He described the palace as more magnificent than the Persian palaces of **Susa** and **Ecbatana**, noting its wooden fortifications and grand stone pillars.
 
• Historical evidence suggests that while the pillars were stone, the roof and floor of the **80-pillar hall** were made of **wood**, which is why much of the structure perished due to fire and environmental factors over **2,000 years**.
 
 
 
• **Influence of Foreign Styles:**
 
 
• Scholars often note a resemblance between the **80-pillar hall** and the **Achaemenid** architecture of **Persia**, specifically the **Hall of a Hundred Columns** at **Persepolis**.
 
• However, the **Mauryan** pillars were **monolithic** (carved from a single stone), unlike the Persian pillars which were constructed in segments.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Kumrahar:**
 
 
• The site of **Kumrahar** is not only famous for the hall but also for other findings like the **Arogya Vihara** (an ancient hospital-monastery) and the **Anand Bihar**.
 
• These findings highlight **Pataliputra** as a major center for administration, religion, and healthcare during **ancient India**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Rulers Mentioned:**

 
 
• **Samudragupta** and **Chandragupta I** belonged to the **Gupta Dynasty** (ruling roughly between **319 CE and 540 CE**). Their architecture focused more on early **Hindu temples** and **cave shrines**, such as the **Udayagiri caves**.
 
• **Harshavardhana** (reigned **606 CE to 647 CE**) was a ruler of the **Pushyabhuti Dynasty** with his capital at **Kannauj**. His era is noted for the support of **Nalanda University** rather than the 80-pillar hall of Pataliputra.
 
 
 
• **Technical Features:**
 
 
• The pillars of the hall were approximately **10 meters** in height and were buried deep into the ground to provide stability for the massive structure above.
 
• The use of **stone** for royal buildings was a transition from the earlier extensive use of **timber** in the **pre-Mauryan** era.

questions.question: Which country has the largest reserve of iron ore in Asia?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **India** is endowed with the largest reserves of **iron ore** in **Asia**. The country possesses approximately **95%** of the total **haematite** and **magnetite** reserves of the continent.
 
• The iron ore found in **India** is of superior quality, particularly the **haematite** variety, which contains about **60% to 70%** metallic iron. This makes it highly sought after in the international market.
 
• Major iron ore belts in **India** include the **Odisha-Jharkhand belt**, **Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur belt**, **Ballari-Chitradurga-Chikkamagaluru-Tumakuru belt**, and the **Maharashtra-Goa belt**.
 
• As per the **Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM)**, the state of **Odisha** is the leading producer and also holds a significant portion of the country's **haematite** reserves.
 
• The high-grade **magnetite** ores, which have **magnetic** properties, are found primarily in **Karnataka** (Kudremukh mines), **Andhra Pradesh**, and **Tamil Nadu**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Iron Ore:**

 
 
• **Haematite**: Known as "Red Ore," it has **60-70%** metallic content. It is the most important industrial iron ore in **India**.
 
• **Magnetite**: Known as "Black Ore," it has the highest iron content (up to **72%**) and possesses excellent **magnetic** qualities, useful in the electrical industry.
 
• **Limonite** and **Siderite**: These are inferior quality ores with lower iron content, ranging from **40% to 60%**.
 
 
 
• **Status of Other Countries:**
 
 
• **China**: While **China** is the world's largest producer and consumer of iron ore, its domestic reserves are often of **lower grade** (low iron content), requiring it to import high-grade ore from **Australia** and **Brazil**.
 
• **Russia**: It holds some of the world's largest total reserves, but much of its massive **Kursk Magnetic Anomaly** and Siberian deposits are geographically categorized under **Europe** or **Eurasia** rather than exclusively **Asia**.
 
• **Iran**: It possesses significant iron ore reserves, particularly in the **Yazd** and **Kerman** provinces, but they are smaller in scale compared to **India**.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• In terms of **global production** as of **2023**, **Australia** and **Brazil** lead the world, followed by **China** and **India**.
 
• **India** exports a large quantity of its iron ore to countries like **Japan**, **South Korea**, and **China** through major ports like **Visakhapatnam**, **Paradip**, and **Marmagao**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Industrial Use**: Iron ore is the basic mineral and the backbone of **industrial development**. It is the primary raw material for the **Iron and Steel Industry**.
 
• **Mining Areas**: In **India**, the **Bailadila** mine in **Chhattisgarh** is famous for its high-grade **haematite** which was originally developed for export to **Japan**.
 
• **Geological Surveys**: Regular surveys by the **Geological Survey of India (GSI)** continue to identify new deposits in **Rajasthan** and **Maharashtra**, further solidifying **India's** position in the mineral sector.

• In recognition of his contribution to **Indian Classical Music**, he was awarded the **Padma Shri** in **1988**, the **Padma Bhushan** in **2002**, and the **Padma Vibhushan** in **2023** by the **Government of India**.
 
• He was a child prodigy who began touring by the **age of 12** and later moved to the **United States** in **1970**, which marked the beginning of his international career and collaborations with **Western** musicians.
 
• **Zakir Hussain** has won multiple **Grammy Awards**. His album **Planet Drum**, co-produced with **Mickey Hart**, won the first-ever **Grammy for Best World Music Album** in **1992**. In **2024**, he made history by winning **three Grammys** in a single night.

• **Musical Instruments and Famous Maestros**:

 
 
• **Sitar**: It is a plucked stringed instrument used in **Hindustani classical music**. Prominent players include **Pandit Ravi Shankar**, **Ustad Vilayat Khan**, and **Nikhil Banerjee**.
 
• **Tabla**: A pair of twin hand drums from the **Indian subcontinent**. It is the principal percussion instrument in **Hindustani** music. Other famous players include **Ustad Allah Rakha**, **Pandit Kishan Maharaj**, and **Anindo Chatterjee**.
 
• **Flute (Bansuri)**: A side-blown flute made from a single hollow shaft of **bamboo**. The most celebrated maestro of the **Bansuri** is **Pandit Hariprasad Chaurasia**. Another notable name is **Pannalal Ghosh**.
 
• **Violin**: While it is a **Western** instrument, it has been adapted into **Indian Classical music**, especially in the **Carnatic** tradition. Renowned Indian violinists include **L. Subramaniam**, **T.N. Krishnan**, and **M.S. Gopalakrishnan**.
 
 
 
• **The Punjab Gharana**: **Ustad Zakir Hussain** represents the **Punjab Gharana** of **Tabla** playing, which is known for its intricate and powerful rhythmic patterns, often influenced by **Pakhawaj** traditions.
 
• **Fusion Music**: He is a founding member of the famous world music fusion band **Shakti**, along with **John McLaughlin** and **L. Shankar**. This group is credited with bridging the gap between **Indian** and **Western** musical styles.

• **Global Recognition**: In **1999**, he was awarded the **National Endowment for the Arts' National Heritage Fellowship**, the highest honor given to traditional artists in the **United States**.
 
• **Collaborations**: Throughout his career, he has collaborated with a diverse range of artists including **George Harrison**, **Yo-Yo Ma**, and **Van Morrison**, showcasing the versatility of the **Tabla** on the global stage.
 
• **Recent Achievements**: In **2024**, **Zakir Hussain** and the band **Shakti** won the **Grammy** for **Best Global Music Album** for their latest release, **This Moment**.
